newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam grants second licence to foreign law firms.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam grants second licence to foreign law firms.

text.p: Vietnam granted 12 foreign law firms licences to open second branches last week, lifting a threat that some would have to close offices in the country's two main cities.
Foreign lawyers said on Wednesday that three firms new to the country had been granted branch licences in Ho Chi Minh City.

Twelve others were given the nod on second branches in either Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City, ending a period of uncertainty for many whose non-renewable representative office licences were coming up to expiry.

One firm, U.S.-based Baker and Mckenzie, had stopped operating in Hanoi because its representative office licence there had already expired. Another, Sinclair Roche and Temperley of Britain, would have had to close its doors in Hanoi by the end of this month.
"If the government hadn't done this there would have been an outcry," said Milton Lawson, an international lawyer at Sinclair Roche and Temperley.
Foreign lawyers, who lobbied hard for permission to open second branches, say doing business in Vietnam is tough because of the communist government's concern about protecting domestic firms.
Foreign law companies each had one representative office upgraded to a branch office earlier this year, which gave them the right to conduct business and make profits.
But despite their new status, foreign firms are still barred from advising on Vietnamese law, which includes explaining or interpreting and drafting contracts with an element of local law.

Lawyers say that is not a major obstacle to doing business because foreign law firms can still work behind the scenes, drafting opinions on contracts and loan transactions which are then signed off by Vietnamese law firms.
More worrying is the question of how much tax law firms will pay now that they have been drawn into the tax net by becoming branches.

Last year the finance ministry proposed a swingeing profit tax rate equal to 20 percent of receipts in addition to the normal service industry turnover tax of four percent. Both foreign lawyers and diplomats protested to the government.

So far there has been no ruling on what tax regime will apply to foreign law firms. However, one lawyer said he believed the government was ready to back-track, imposing a 25 percent profit tax as it does with accountancy firms.
